tp.name: What Is Toilet Paper?
tp.title: Ingredient Dictionary: What Is Toilet Paper?

puzzles.note: A wax from Brazilian palm leaves. It gives gummies their shine — and it's also a classic ingredient in car wax and shoe polish.
A sugar alcohol that keeps the paste moist and sweet. It's the same sweetener found in sugar-free gum and candy.
That's plain table salt. Shampoo makers add it to make the liquid thicker.
A waxy grease that comes from sheep's wool. Sheep make it to waterproof their coats.
An emulsifying salt that makes slices melt perfectly smooth. With all the extras, many are legally labeled "cheese product," not cheese.
A preservative that's a common skin allergen. The EU banned it from leave-on cosmetics, but it still shows up in rinse-off products and cleaners.
A preservative that grabs onto metals so flavors don't go stale. Doctors use the same compound to treat lead poisoning.
A fatty acid from plant or animal fat. It's also what makes candles and bar soap hard.
An emulsifier that keeps oil and water mixed. You'll find the same family of ingredients in lotions and creams.
The same gases used in camping stoves. In a can, they're what puff the cream into foam.
Also known as laughing gas — the same gas a dentist uses. It whips the cream as it leaves the can.

ingredients: Hydrogenated vegetable oil (coconut and palm kernel)
puzzles.note: It's sixth on the list. The tub is mostly water, oil and syrup — cream makes up only a tiny part.
Despite the name, it's not drying like rubbing alcohol. It's a waxy "fatty alcohol" from coconut or palm that makes conditioner creamy.
It gives cola its tang. It's also the main ingredient in many rust removers.
The same acid your stomach makes to digest food. Never mix it with bleach — together they release toxic gas.
That's about 43 proof — stronger than most wine. It's why the classic version burns.
Made from pine tree rosin. It keeps the flavor oils from floating to the top of the bottle.
Ammonia dissolved in water — it's what cuts the streaks. Never mix it with bleach.
A preservative that stops fats from going rancid. The same antioxidant is also added to rubber, plastics and jet fuel.
The same dye used in candy. Dogs don't care what color their treats are — the color is there for the humans.
There's no bacon in them at all. They're crunchy bits of flavored, colored soy.
A preservative first developed to stabilize rubber. The EU suspended it as an animal feed additive in 2017.

ingredients: Hydrogenated vegetable oil (coconut and/or palm kernel)
puzzles.note: A milk protein that keeps the oil blended into your coffee — even though the jar says "non-dairy." Labeling rules allow it.
The same cornstarch in your pantry, under its Latin name. Many brands switched to it from talc.
The first three ingredients are flammable fuel gases. Let it settle before you go near a curling iron or flame.
An anti-foaming silicone — the same family as the dimethicone in hair conditioner and lotion.
The wrapper that dissolves in the wash. Pods look like candy, so keep them locked away from kids.
Baking soda plus acid — the same fizz as a science-fair volcano or a fizzy antacid tablet.
The second-stage acid that makes "double-acting" powder rise again in the oven. Aluminum-free versions exist.
Flavor boosters that make MSG taste many times stronger. They're often made from yeast or fish.
Better known as Epsom salt. It's also sold as a laxative and as garden fertilizer.
Named after bulls (Latin taurus) because it was first found in ox bile. Today it's made in a lab.
It keeps the syrup smooth. It's also the base of "pet-safer" antifreeze.
A secret blend that can include synthetic rubber and polyvinyl acetate — a plastic also used in white wood glue.
Yes, fish oil — in a baby cream. It's there to soothe skin.
A meat paste made by pressing chicken bones through a sieve under high pressure.
Pet food labels list water first when it's the biggest ingredient — the can is mostly water.
A common label trick: splitting the sweetener into two kinds pushes each one lower on the list.
The same alcohol found in drinks — denatured with bitter additives so nobody drinks it.
The hold in hair gel. It was used during World War II as a blood plasma substitute.
A natural gelling fiber from apple peels and citrus rinds. It's what turns juice into jelly.
Also called lye. It's the same chemical used to make soap — and to give soft pretzels their shiny brown crust.
A dye that glows blue under UV light so white clothes look whiter. It doesn't clean anything — it just changes how fabric reflects light.
The same acid in ant stings. Its name comes from formica, Latin for ant.
Washing soda bonded with hydrogen peroxide. In water it releases oxygen bubbles — the "oxygen bleach" in stain removers.
The compound that makes oranges smell like oranges. Indoors it can react with ozone in the air and form small amounts of formaldehyde.
Basically ground-up chalk or limestone — the gritty scrubber. It's also the main ingredient in many antacid tablets.
A preservative that works by slowly releasing tiny amounts of formaldehyde.
That's added vitamin C. It lets the box say "good source of vitamin C" even though it's mostly syrup and sugar.
Where the bright orange comes from. Many brands swapped artificial dyes like Yellow 5 and 6 for spices.
The first two ingredients. They taste like candy, which is exactly why the bottle has a child-proof cap.
Third on the list — after water and syrup. Many "juice drinks" are only about 10% juice.
Lye. It clears clogs by turning hair and grease into soap that rinses away. It can burn skin and eyes.
The sweet syrup is bait. Ants carry it home and share it, and the borax slowly works through the colony.
The sheet itself is plastic fabric. It's a carrier that melts softener and fragrance onto your clothes in the heat.
Cats can't make enough of it on their own, so it's added — the same ingredient that's in energy drinks.
Also called Dutch-process cocoa. The alkali darkens the color and mellows the taste — and strips out much of cocoa's natural antioxidants.
A silicone added to frying oil so it doesn't foam up. It's the same family of silicone used in caulk and conditioner.
A bright red color made from crushed cochineal bugs. It's natural — but it's not vegetarian, and some people are allergic to it.
There's no maple at all. "Table syrup" is corn syrup colored brown and flavored to taste like maple.
Two kinds of sugar come first. The orange comes from flavoring and two synthetic dyes — not from oranges.
An aluminum salt that forms tiny plugs in sweat ducts so you sweat less. Deodorant alone just covers the smell.
The most bitter chemical known. It's added so anyone who takes a sip — especially a child — spits it right out.
A chemical UV filter. The FDA has asked makers for more safety data, and Europe now limits how much can be used.
A plastic-like film that dries stiff on each hair. That's the "hold."
Purified rust. Red, yellow and black iron oxides are mixed to match skin tones.
Proteins that break down stains the way your stomach breaks down food — protease eats grass and blood, amylase eats starch.
Lye. It turns baked-on grease into soap so it wipes away — and it can burn skin and eyes, so gloves on.
A "quat" disinfectant. It kills germs — and leaves a film behind, which is why labels say to rinse food surfaces.
A silicone that leaves a glossy, slippery film — the same ingredient that makes hair conditioner feel smooth.
Soap made from beef fat (tallow) mixed with lye. Old-fashioned soap has been made this way for centuries.
A ring-shaped sugar molecule made from corn starch. Odor molecules get trapped inside the ring — then fragrance covers the rest.
It makes water slide off dishes in a sheet instead of drying in spots. The label doesn't have to say exactly which one.
A mild foaming agent from coconut oil — yet it was named "Allergen of the Year" in 2004 by the American Contact Dermatitis Society.
A preservative in many baby products. France advises against it in wipes and creams used on the diaper area of children under 3.
It strengthens teeth, but kids shouldn't swallow it. That's why young children get just a rice-grain or pea-sized smear.
A seaweed thickener that keeps the cocoa from sinking to the bottom. Scientists still debate its effect on the gut.
A paraben preservative. The EU limits how much can be used in cosmetics and bans it in leave-on products for babies' diaper areas.
The foaming detergent that makes mountains of bubbles. Pediatricians warn long bubble baths can irritate young children's skin.
It tastes sweet, which makes it dangerous to pets and kids. A bittering agent is added so it tastes awful.
Wood alcohol. It keeps the fluid from freezing — and swallowing even a little can cause blindness.
A petroleum wax. When it burns, it gives off soot along with whatever is in the fragrance.
Sprayed into the air to kill some airborne germs. It's also used to dry out natural gas in pipelines.
It actually heats up as it dissolves, so it melts ice fast. It can also dry out and crack pets' paws.
The bright white in white paint — the same mineral used to whiten toothpaste and candy coatings.

puzzles.statement: Most toilet paper starts out as trees.
puzzles.note: Most rolls are made from wood pulp, much of it from virgin forests. Bamboo and recycled paper are the main alternatives.

puzzles.statement: Toilet paper is naturally white.
puzzles.note: Wood pulp is brown. Toilet paper is bleached to make it white — usually with chlorine dioxide.

puzzles.statement: Scientists have found PFAS "forever chemicals" in toilet paper.
puzzles.note: A 2023 study tested toilet paper from around the world and found PFAS in it. PFAS can be used in paper-making.

puzzles.statement: Recycled toilet paper can contain traces of BPA.
puzzles.note: BPA coats many thermal cash-register receipts. When receipts get recycled into paper, traces can carry over.

puzzles.statement: "Flushable" wipes break down in pipes just like toilet paper.
puzzles.note: Toilet paper is made to fall apart in water within seconds. Wipes hold together, so they clog pipes and sewers.

puzzles.statement: Toilet paper is designed to fall apart when it gets wet.
puzzles.note: Its fibers are short and only lightly bonded, so it breaks up in water instead of clogging your pipes.

puzzles.statement: Packaged toilet paper has been sold in the US since the 1850s.
puzzles.note: Joseph Gayetty sold flat sheets of "medicated paper" in 1857. Rolls came a few decades later.

puzzles.statement: Most people in the world use toilet paper.
puzzles.note: Much of the world — including large parts of Asia, the Middle East and southern Europe — mainly uses water instead.

puzzles.statement: The average American uses more than 100 rolls of toilet paper a year.
puzzles.note: Estimates put it around 140 rolls per person per year — among the highest in the world.

puzzles.statement: Brown, unbleached toilet paper is dirtier than white toilet paper.
puzzles.note: The color comes from skipping the bleach, not from dirt. Unbleached paper just skips a chemical step.

puzzles.statement: Scented toilet paper can irritate sensitive skin.
puzzles.note: Added fragrance is one of the most common causes of skin irritation, and toilet paper touches very sensitive skin.

puzzles.statement: The original 1891 toilet-roll patent drawing shows the paper hanging "over," not "under."
puzzles.note: Seth Wheeler's patent drawing shows the loose end hanging over the front of the roll. Debate settled?

puzzles.statement: A 1930s toilet paper brand advertised itself as "splinter-free."
puzzles.note: Early paper could contain bits of wood. One brand made "splinter-free" a selling point in the 1930s.

puzzles.statement: Most toilet paper sold in the US is made from recycled paper.
puzzles.note: Most US toilet paper is made from new (virgin) wood pulp. Recycled rolls are a small share of sales.

puzzles.statement: Toilet paper sheets have gotten smaller over the years.
puzzles.note: Many brands have quietly shrunk sheet sizes and sheet counts while keeping the price the same.

puzzles.statement: Bamboo toilet paper is always chemical-free.
puzzles.note: Bamboo still has to be pulped and is often bleached. Testers have even found PFAS markers in some bamboo brands.

puzzles.statement: In March 2020, US toilet paper sales more than doubled in some weeks.
puzzles.note: Panic buying at the start of the pandemic sent sales soaring for weeks and emptied store shelves.

puzzles.statement: "Two-ply" means two layers of paper pressed together.
puzzles.note: Each sheet is two thin layers bonded together, which makes it softer and stronger than one thick layer.

puzzles.statement: Ancient Romans used a sponge on a stick instead of toilet paper.
puzzles.note: It was called a tersorium — a sea sponge on a stick, rinsed in water or vinegar and shared.

puzzles.statement: Toilet paper companies must list the chemicals used to make it.
puzzles.note: There's no ingredient label on toilet paper. Makers don't have to disclose what goes into it.
